historical_timeline.summary: Born near present Prague, Oklahoma, on the Sac and Fox reservation.
Olympic gold medals in the pentathlon and decathlon in Stockholm.
Named the greatest athlete of the half-century in an Associated Press poll.
Operation for lip cancer in a Philadelphia hospital.
Died of a heart attack in Lomita, California.
Recognized by the International Olympic Committee as co-winner of the 1912 events.
Restored as sole winner of the 1912 pentathlon and decathlon.

claims.statement: James Francis Thorpe was born a twin on the Sac and Fox reservation near present Prague, Oklahoma, to Hiram and Charlotte Vieux Thorpe. His Sac and Fox name, Wa-tho-huck, means "Bright Path." He is usually considered Sac and Fox and was brought up as a member of the Sac and Fox tribe; he also had Potawatomi, Kickapoo, Menominee, Irish and French ancestry. The Oklahoma Historical Society gives his birth as May 28, 1888, noting that his estate cites 1887; another reference work gives May 22, 1887.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Birth date uncertain; May 28, 1888 is used (see sources.md). His identity as a Sac and Fox man anchors the culturally appropriate care options.

source_links.locator: b. 22 May 1887; brought up as a member of the Sac and Fox tribe

claims.statement: His twin brother, Charles, died of pneumonia just short of their eighth birthday; his mother died when he was twelve and his father when he was sixteen.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; causes of his parents' deaths are not recorded in the cited source.

source_links.locator: death of his twin at age eight; both parents died while he was at boarding school

claims.statement: He attended federal boarding schools, including the Sac and Fox Indian Agency School, Haskell Institute, and from 1903 the Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania, where he became a track and football star.

source_links.locator: sent to the Carlisle Institute at sixteen

claims.statement: At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm he won gold medals in the pentathlon and decathlon. In January 1913 the Amateur Athletic Union stripped him of his medals because he had played semiprofessional baseball; in 1982 the International Olympic Committee recognized him as co-winner, and on July 15, 2022 it restored him as sole winner of both events.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Social history only; the Pro Football Hall of Fame dates the co-champion recognition to 1992, and the Oklahoma Historical Society and Smithsonian Magazine to 1982, which is used.

source_links.locator: October 1982, replica medals delivered to his family
restored as co-champion; named sole winner in 2022

claims.statement: He played major-league baseball from 1913 to 1919 and professional football into 1928, and was the first president of the American Professional Football Association, the forerunner of the National Football League. Afterwards he worked as a film extra and in construction, as a security guard and ditch digger, at the Ford plant in Dearborn during the Second World War, and in the Merchant Marine in 1945; he became a critic of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, lectured widely, and worked to inspire American Indians.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern work and sun-exposure history; his public speaking and service to Native communities are recorded as strengths.

source_links.locator: security guard, construction worker and ditch digger; lecture circuit

claims.statement: He reportedly had an alcohol problem; one reference work states that excessive drinking began at Carlisle and troubled him for the rest of his life and frustrated his attempts at a stable married life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded factually and only as history; the modern episode screens for alcohol use without assuming it.

claims.statement: In 1951 he was treated for lip cancer as a charity patient in a Philadelphia hospital, where he had an operation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode and its index age. The type of cancer is not recorded in the cited sources.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 63-year-old Sac and Fox man, a former Olympic and professional athlete, with a non-healing lower-lip lesion and chronic coronary disease: biopsy of a suspicious lip lesion, squamous cell carcinoma of the lip staged and treated by excision with clear margins, sun and tobacco exposure history, surveillance and second-primary prevention on the NCCN head and neck guideline; perioperative cardiac assessment for low-risk surgery with aspirin continued; secondary prevention after a heart attack (aspirin, a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe to the LDL goal, a beta-blocker for angina, blood pressure) and cardiac rehabilitation on the 2023 AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline and the CMID ischemic heart disease monograph; and care options offered with respect, including coordination with Sac and Fox Nation or Indian Health Service programs, without assuming his preferences.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Thorpe returns one week after his first visit and is seen the same day by Dr. Ferrante of otolaryngology (head and neck surgery). The biopsy site on his lip has healed over. The pathology shows invasive, well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. He started aspirin, atorvastatin and metoprolol a week ago and has had one episode of chest tightness walking up the hill to the ball field, which eased with rest; he did not need nitroglycerin. He had his echocardiogram this morning. He feels the metoprolol a little in his legs on the first days but less now. He asked many questions about the operation and how his lip will look and work afterwards, and whether he can keep coaching.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Thorpe returns two weeks after V-excision of the lower lip cancer by Dr. Ferrante. The CT of the neck before surgery showed no enlarged or abnormal lymph nodes. He took acetaminophen for three days after the operation and needed nothing stronger. The stitches were removed last week. His lip feels a little tight but he can whistle, drink from a cup and speak clearly. He has had no chest tightness since the first week of his medicines and has not used nitroglycerin. He took aspirin throughout and had only slight oozing on the first night. He is keen to start cardiac rehabilitation.

assessment.assessment: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip, 1.2 cm, with no palpable nodes: clinical T1 N0 (AJCC 8th edition, lip and oral cavity). Surgery is the preferred treatment. A V-excision with 5 to 10 mm clinical margins and frozen-section control of the margins, closed directly, removes up to a third of the lower lip with good function and appearance. Lower lip cancers of this size rarely spread to the neck; a contrast CT of the neck is reasonable before surgery to stage it, and elective neck dissection is not needed if the final depth of invasion is small, generally under 4 mm, with clear margins. Radiation is an alternative but is not preferred for a small, resectable lesion

assessment.display: Chronic coronary disease with stable angina
assessment.assessment: An excision under local anesthesia is a low-risk operation. With stable angina, an ejection fraction of 55%, and no heart failure, no further cardiac testing is needed. Aspirin should be continued because bleeding from a lip excision is easily controlled, and metoprolol should not be stopped

recommendations: Contrast CT of the neck before surgery
V-excision of the lower lip cancer under local anesthesia with 5 to 10 mm margins and frozen-section margin control, with primary closure, in about two weeks
No elective neck dissection if the final depth of invasion is small and the margins are clear; re-excision if a margin is involved
Continue aspirin 81 mg and metoprolol through surgery; acetaminophen for pain afterwards

Surveillance by history and examination of the lips, mouth and neck every 1 to 3 months in the first year, every 2 to 6 months in the second, every 4 to 8 months in years 3 to 5, then yearly; imaging only for symptoms or findings
Daily lip balm with sunscreen and a hat, yearly skin examination, staying tobacco-free, and a dental check-up
Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT if he is eligible, because of his smoking history
